lesson.title: Naming the Data Your Program Works With
lesson.summary: A variable is a name that a program uses to refer to a value stored in memory, letting code work with data by name instead of retyping literal values everywhere.
lesson.body:
Every useful program needs to keep track of information as it runs, whether that is a score in a game, a temperature reading, or a piece of text a user typed. A variable is the mechanism programming languages provide for this: a name chosen by the programmer that refers to some value the program is currently working with. Instead of writing the number 85 over and over throughout a program, you can store it once under a name like score and refer to score from then on, which is both easier to read and easier to change later, since updating one assignment updates every place that uses the name.

In Python specifically, it helps to think of a variable not as a labeled box holding a value, but as a name tag attached to an object that lives somewhere in memory. When you write score = 85, Python creates an integer object representing the value 85 somewhere in memory, and the name score is bound to that object. This distinction matters more once you start working with values that can change internally, but even for simple values like numbers, it explains a lot of Python's behavior, including why assignment works the way it does, which the next chapter explores in detail.

Consider this short example:

score = 85
print(score)
score = score + 10
print(score)

Tracing through it: the first line creates the integer object 85 and binds the name score to it. The first print(score) looks up what score currently refers to and displays 85. The third line evaluates score + 10 first, which means looking up score's current value, 85, and adding 10 to get 95, and then binds the name score to this new integer object 95. The original object 85 is not modified, a brand new object 95 exists, and score simply now points at the new one instead of the old one. The second print(score) therefore displays 95.

Without variables, programs could only ever work with fixed, literal values typed directly into the code, which would make it impossible to build anything that responds to changing input, remembers a result to use later, or performs the same calculation on different data. A program that always computed 85 + 10 with those exact literal numbers could never be reused for a different starting score, but a program built around the name score can run the same logic on any value that gets bound to that name.

Since you already know, from Python Language, that Python is dynamically typed, it is worth restating here in the context of variables specifically: a variable name itself carries no fixed type, only the object it currently refers to has a type, which is why the same name can be bound to an integer at one point in a program and a string at another point without Python raising an error. This is exactly why the box metaphor for variables is misleading in Python. A labeled box suggests a fixed container that always holds a value of the same kind and shape, while a name tag suggests something that can be moved from object to object freely, which is much closer to how Python variables actually behave, and which sets up the precise mechanics of assignment covered in the next chapter.
